a: took firm hold of his kingdom
t: Chronicles skips the struggle for the throne
p: Kings spends two chapters on how Solomon won and secured the throne. Chronicles moves straight to a settled kingdom.
b: In 1 Kings 1–2 Solomon becomes king through a palace struggle with his brother Adonijah, and then has Adonijah, Joab and Shimei put to death. Chronicles leaves all of that out. 1 Chronicles 23:1 and 29:22–25 had already shown a smooth handover, with all Israel and all David's sons pledging loyalty. Many critical scholars (Japhet, Williamson) see a deliberate picture: David and Solomon form one ideal reign, and nothing should cloud the Temple builder. Traditional readers answer that Chronicles assumes its readers know Kings and tells only what serves its purpose. The verb hitchazzeq, "take firm hold," is a favorite of Chronicles for a king who has made his rule secure (12:13; 13:21; 17:1; 21:4).

a: The LORD his God
p: Capital letters mark God's personal name, YHWH, which Jews do not pronounce.
b: Where the Hebrew has the four letters YHWH, God's own name, this translation writes "the LORD" in capitals, as most English Bibles do. Jewish readers have long said Adonai, "Lord," in its place out of reverence, and the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the Septuagint, used kyrios, "Lord." When the Hebrew has Adonai itself, the Plain English Translation writes "Lord" in ordinary letters. "LORD God" stands for YHWH Elohim, as in 1:9 and 6:41.

a: the high place at Gibeon
t: Why worship at a high place?
p: Kings apologizes for worship at a high place. Chronicles explains it: the tabernacle of Moses stood at Gibeon.
b: Kings introduces the Gibeon visit with a note of unease: "the people kept offering sacrifices at the high places" and Solomon "too sacrificed at the high places" (1 Kings 3:2–3). Chronicles turns the trip into a proper act of worship by the whole assembly, because "God's tent of meeting was there." It had said the same earlier: "the LORD's tabernacle, the one Moses made in the wilderness, stood at the high place in Gibeon, with the altar of burnt offering" (1 Chronicles 21:29). In Chronicles the ark and the tabernacle were in two places until the Temple joined them again (5:5). Gibeon is el-Jib, about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

a: Moses the servant of the LORD
p: The Hebrew eved means 'servant' or 'slave.' Here it is an honored title.
b: Eved can mean a slave, a royal official, or a worshiper who belongs to God. "The servant of the LORD" is a title of honor given to Moses (Deuteronomy 34:5; Joshua 1:1) and later to David (6:42). The Plain English Translation says "servant" when the word describes an official or a worshiper, as with Hiram's "servants" (2:8) and the people Solomon would not make "a slave" (8:9), where the sense is forced labor.

a: Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur
p: The altar at Gibeon is the very one Bezalel made in the wilderness. Solomon's Temple will copy Bezalel's work.
b: Bezalel was the craftsman filled with God's Spirit to make the tabernacle and its bronze altar (Exodus 31:1–5; Exodus 38:1–2). Only Chronicles names him outside the Torah, and it also places him in Judah's family tree (1 Chronicles 2:20). Naming him here ties Solomon's first act of worship to Moses' tabernacle. In 2:13–14 Solomon gets a craftsman of his own, Huram-abi, whose description echoes Bezalel and his helper Oholiab.

a: Solomon and the assembly sought it
p: The Hebrew 'sought it/him' can mean they came to the altar, or that they consulted the LORD there.
b: The verb darash with the pronoun ending -hu can mean "sought it" (the altar) or "sought him" (the LORD). Many translations take it as the altar, the place of worship. Others read "inquired of him," since "seeking" the LORD is a key idea in Chronicles: Saul died because he did not seek the LORD (1 Chronicles 10:14), and the good kings are those who seek him (11:16; 14:4; 15:12). Either way, Chronicles begins Solomon's reign with the whole people seeking God at the proper altar, the opposite of Saul. See 12:14.

a: That night God showed himself to Solomon
p: Kings says God came to Solomon 'in a dream.' Chronicles leaves the dream out.
b: In Kings the scene opens and closes with a dream (1 Kings 3:5, 3:15). Chronicles keeps the night but drops the word "dream." Some scholars think the change reflects a wider reserve in later writings about dreams as a way of hearing God. Others think it is only shortening, since Chronicles keeps Solomon's return to Jerusalem (1:13) but drops his sacrifice and feast before the ark (1 Kings 3:15) and the famous case of the two mothers (1 Kings 3:16–28). The effect is that the meeting with God reads like a vision at the holy place rather than a private sleep.

a: loyal love
p: Hesed is the faithful love that keeps a commitment. This site renders it 'loyal love' everywhere.
b: Hesed is love shown in faithfulness to a relationship or a promise: kindness that can be counted on. Older English said "mercy" or "lovingkindness." In Chronicles it is God's covenant faithfulness to David (6:14; 6:42) and the refrain of Temple worship, "for his loyal love is forever" (5:13; 7:3; 7:6).

a: may your word to David my father hold true
p: Solomon asks God to confirm the promise of a son on David's throne, the promise of 1 Chronicles 17.
b: The verb is ye'amen, "be made firm, prove true," from the root of "amen." It picks up David's own prayer: "let the word you spoke about your servant and his house be made sure forever" (1 Chronicles 17:23), where the same verb is used. Kings has Solomon recall God's loyal love to David "as he walked before you in truth" (1 Kings 3:6). Chronicles turns that into a request that the promise be fulfilled in Solomon. The same plea returns in the Temple prayer (6:17).

a: wisdom and knowledge
p: Kings has Solomon ask for 'a heart that listens.' Chronicles uses a pair of words common in later Hebrew.
b: In Kings Solomon asks for "a heart that listens, so he can judge your people" (1 Kings 3:9). Chronicles has chokhmah umadda', "wisdom and knowledge." Madda' is a late word, found otherwise in Daniel 1:4, 1:17 and Ecclesiastes 10:20. In Daniel, a book of the Persian or Greek period, it is the gift Daniel and his friends bring to the Babylonian court. The phrase "go out ... and come back in" means to lead the people in everyday affairs and in war (Numbers 27:17; 1 Samuel 18:16).

a: No king before you had so much, and none after you will.
p: Kings ends God's answer with a condition. Chronicles leaves it out, and keeps the conditions for chapter 7.
b: In Kings God adds, "If you walk in my ways ... I will also lengthen your days" (1 Kings 3:14). Chronicles omits the condition here. It also turns Kings' words about "riches and glory" into the three-part "riches, treasure and glory." Nekhasim, "treasure, possessions," is a rare word, found in Joshua 22:8 but common in late Hebrew and Aramaic (Ecclesiastes 5:19; Ecclesiastes 6:2). The conditions do come, but later and in full, after the Temple is built (7:17–22). Readers have seen in this an emphasis of Chronicles: wisdom and wealth are God's free gift for building the Temple, while blessing over time depends on faithfulness.

a: Solomon built up a force of chariots and horsemen
t: Horses at the start and the end
p: These four verses appear again, shorter and altered, at 9:25–28, framing Solomon's whole reign.
b: 1:14–17 copy 1 Kings 10:26–29, which in Kings comes near the end of Solomon's reign, just before his sins. Chronicles moves the passage to the start, to show God's promise of riches (1:12) coming true at once, and repeats it in shorter, altered form at 9:25–28. Readers of Deuteronomy will remember that the king "must not get himself many horses, or send the people back to Egypt to get more horses" (Deuteronomy 17:16). Kings may be hinting at that warning (see the note on 1 Kings 10:26). Chronicles, by placing the lists as proof of blessing, seems not to read them as criticism.

a: He based them
p: Chronicles has 'he placed them.' Kings' Hebrew has 'he led them,' and the site's Kings page renders both 'based.'
b: Chronicles has vayyannichem, "he placed (stationed) them," here and at 9:25. 1 Kings 10:26 has vayyanchem, "he led them," which differs by one letter. Most scholars think Chronicles has the better text and Kings a slip; the site's Kings page already gives the sense "based."

a: silver and gold
p: Kings says Solomon made silver as common as stones. Chronicles adds gold here, but not in the repeat at 9:27.
b: 1 Kings 10:27 has only silver, and so does 9:27, Chronicles' own second copy of this verse. Here Chronicles adds "and gold." Most scholars see a deliberate heightening at the start of the reign, as a sign of the riches God has just promised (1:12); others think "gold" crept in by copying. Either way the extra word belongs to Chronicles.
orig: אֶת־הַכֶּסֶף וְאֶת־הַזָּהָב ('the silver and the gold')

a: out of Que
p: The KJV reads 'linen yarn.' The word is a place name: Que, which is Cilicia in southern Turkey.
b: The Hebrew miqqewe' (Kings writes it miqweh, ending in he; Chronicles ends it with aleph) was read by older interpreters as miqweh, "a gathering," and the Latin Vulgate and the KJV turned it into "linen yarn." Assyrian records name a land called Que (Assyrian Qu'e) in Cilicia, famous for horses, and almost all modern translations read the place name. Some scholars also think "Egypt" here hides Musri, a land in the same region. See the note on 1 Kings 10:28.

a: a house for his own royal rule
t: The palace that is never described
p: Chronicles mentions Solomon's palace three times but never describes it. Kings spends twelve verses on it.
b: Kings interrupts the Temple account to describe Solomon's palace, built over thirteen years, with the House of the Forest of Lebanon and the hall for Pharaoh's daughter (1 Kings 7:1–12). Chronicles names the palace (2:1; 2:12; 7:11; 8:1) but tells nothing about it. Its eyes are on the Temple. Some readers in Kings sense a criticism in the palace's longer building time; Chronicles avoids the comparison entirely.

a: Huram king of Tyre
p: Chronicles spells the king's name Huram. He is the Hiram of Kings and of 1 Chronicles 14:1.
b: Kings calls the king of Tyre Chiram (Hiram); Chronicles writes Churam (Huram), another form of the same name, and the Plain English Translation prints each verse's own form. The bronze worker has the same name: Hiram in Kings (1 Kings 7:13), Huram in Chronicles (4:11; 4:16) and Huram-abi in 2:13. At 4:11 and 9:10 the written Hebrew (Ketiv) has Hiram and the reading tradition (Qere) Huram; the Plain English Translation follows the Qere (see the variants there). In Chronicles Solomon writes first; in Kings Hiram first sends envoys to congratulate him (1 Kings 5:1).

a: the rows of bread will always be laid out
p: Solomon lists the daily, weekly, monthly and yearly worship of the Law. The Temple exists for it.
b: Kings has Solomon say he will build a house for the LORD's name (1 Kings 5:5). Chronicles adds what will happen inside: incense morning and evening (Exodus 30:7–8), the bread set out in rows on the table every Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5–9), and the burnt offerings of Numbers 28–29 for every morning and evening, Sabbath, new moon and feast. The list returns in 8:13, 13:11 and 31:3, and again in Ezra and Nehemiah, where the returned exiles restore exactly these offerings (Ezra 3:4–5; Nehemiah 10:33). For Chronicles' first readers this was the daily life of the rebuilt Temple.

a: The heavens, the heavens above the heavens, are not big enough for him.
t: A house for a God no house can hold
p: Solomon says no house can contain God before he builds one, as he says again in his prayer.
b: These words come from the Temple prayer (6:18; 1 Kings 8:27), and Chronicles also puts them at the start of the project. The tension is deliberate: God cannot be contained, yet he chooses a place for his name. Solomon's answer here is modest: the house is "a place to burn offerings before him," a place for worship rather than a home for a god, as ancient temples were usually thought to be. Stephen quotes a similar thought from Isaiah 66:1 against too much trust in the Temple (Acts 7:47–50).

a: crimson
p: Karmil, 'crimson,' is found only in Chronicles. It seems to be a word borrowed from Persian.
b: Exodus uses tola'at shani, "scarlet" (literally "worm of scarlet," from the insect that gave the dye). Chronicles uses karmil (2:7, 2:14, 3:14), which most scholars trace to Persian kirm, "worm," the same source as English "crimson" and "carmine." It is one of several small clues that the book was written in the Persian period or later. Tekhelet, blue-violet, was a dye made from sea snails, and argaman, purple, came from the same Phoenician coast as Hiram's workers.

a: algum
p: Kings calls this wood almug; Chronicles, algum. No one is sure what tree it was.
b: The two spellings swap two letters, a common kind of variation. In Kings, almug wood comes by ship from Ophir (1 Kings 10:11). Chronicles has algum both from Lebanon here and from Ophir in 9:10. A wood called elammakku is known from Ugarit and Mesopotamia, which fits a tree of Syria or Lebanon. Suggestions include red sandalwood (for the Ophir trade) and a kind of juniper. See the note on 1 Kings 10:11.

a: twenty thousand cors of threshed wheat
p: Chronicles has Solomon pay the woodcutters in wheat, barley, wine and oil. Kings speaks of food for Hiram's household.
b: A cor was a dry measure of roughly 220 liters (about 6 bushels), so 20,000 cors is some 4,400,000 liters of wheat. A bath was a liquid measure of about 22 liters (about 6 gallons). In Kings Solomon gives Hiram wheat and "twenty cors of oil from beaten olives" each year for his household (1 Kings 5:11). Chronicles adds barley and wine, raises the oil to 20,000 baths, and has the payment go to the workers. The Greek of Kings also has 20,000 for the oil (see the variant on 1 Kings 5:11). Japhet suggests Chronicles describes a single payment for the job, Kings a yearly one.

a: It is because of the LORD's love for his people
t: Foreigners who see God's love for Israel
p: Both Hiram and the queen of Sheba say Israel's king is a sign of God's love for his people.
b: Hiram's words match the queen of Sheba's: "Your God loves Israel ... That is why he made you king over them" (9:8). In Chronicles foreign rulers recognize what Israel's God is doing. For readers under Persian rule this mattered: a later foreign king, Cyrus, would also speak of "the LORD, the God of heaven" giving him a charge to build his house (36:23).

a: who made the heavens and the earth
p: Hiram blesses the LORD as maker of heaven and earth, words Kings does not give him.
b: Kings has Hiram say only, "Blessed is the LORD today" (1 Kings 5:7). Chronicles has him confess the God of Israel as Creator, as Melchizedek blessed Abram "by God Most High, maker of heaven and earth" (Genesis 14:19). The phrase is common in the Psalms (Psalm 115:15; Psalm 121:2; Psalm 134:3) and in Persian-period prayers (Nehemiah 9:6). Whether a king of Tyre, who worshiped Baal and Melqart, would speak this way is doubted by many critical scholars; others note that ancient diplomats often praised each other's gods.

a: Huram-abi
p: The name is literally 'Huram my father.' It may be a full name, or a title meaning 'master craftsman.'
b: The Hebrew is leChuram avi; 4:16 has Churam aviv, "Huram his father," which the Plain English Translation translates as it stands. The KJV took it as "of Huram my father's," as if the man belonged to the household of Hiram's father. Most modern readers take abi as part of a name (compare Abiram) or as a title of respect, as when Joseph says God "has made me a father to Pharaoh" (Genesis 45:8), meaning his chief adviser. The Greek (Rahlfs' edition, checked) has "Chiram my father." In Kings the bronze worker is simply Hiram (1 Kings 7:13).

a: His mother came from the daughters of Dan
p: Kings says the craftsman's mother was from Naphtali. Chronicles says Dan, the tribe of Oholiab, Bezalel's helper.
b: Kings: "His mother was a widow from the tribe of Naphtali" (1 Kings 7:14). Chronicles: from Dan. Harmonizers suggest she was born in Dan and married into Naphtali, or that she lived in the northern town of Dan, which lay in Naphtali's area. Many scholars see a deliberate echo: the tabernacle was built by Bezalel of Judah and "Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan" (Exodus 35:34). Chronicles pairs Solomon of Judah with a craftsman from Dan, and gives Huram-abi a skill list close to Bezalel's (Exodus 35:31–35), working in every material, not only bronze as in Kings.

a: to Joppa
p: Ezra uses the same route for the second Temple: cedars from Lebanon by sea to Joppa.
b: Kings does not name the port. Chronicles names Joppa, modern Jaffa, the harbor nearest Jerusalem (about 35 miles or 55 kilometers away). When the exiles rebuilt the Temple, they gave "food, drink and oil to the people of Sidon and Tyre, to bring cedar wood from Lebanon to the sea at Joppa" (Ezra 3:7). The first readers of Chronicles would have heard their own Temple's story in Solomon's. Joppa is also where Jonah boarded his ship (Jonah 1:3) and where Peter saw his vision (Acts 10:5–16).

a: Solomon counted all the foreigners living in the land of Israel
p: Chronicles says the 153,600 laborers were resident foreigners. Kings says Solomon drafted Israelites too.
b: 1 Kings 5:13–14 has Solomon draft thirty thousand Israelites to cut timber in shifts. Chronicles leaves that out and counts only gerim, foreigners living in the land, as David had done (1 Chronicles 22:2). The numbers match: 70,000 + 80,000 + 3,600 = 153,600. Kings has 3,300 foremen (1 Kings 5:16); see the variant on 2:2. Kings itself says elsewhere that Solomon made no Israelite a slave (1 Kings 9:22). Some harmonize: Israelites served short rotations, foreigners permanent labor. Many critical scholars think Chronicles removed a detail that made Solomon look like a harsh master, a complaint that later split the kingdom (10:4). The count recalls David's census of 1 Chronicles 21, though without its guilt.

a: Mount Moriah
t: Moriah: Isaac's mountain and the Temple mount
p: Only here does the Bible name the Temple hill Moriah, linking it with Abraham's offering of Isaac.
b: God told Abraham to go "to the land of Moriah" and offer Isaac "on one of the mountains that I will point out to you" (Genesis 22:2). Abraham named the place "The LORD Will See," and the saying followed, "On the mountain of the LORD it will be seen" (Genesis 22:14). Chronicles names the Temple site "Mount Moriah" and recalls that the LORD "had shown himself" there to David, a play on the same verb ra'ah, "see." Jewish tradition built on this: Josephus (Antiquities 1.226) and the rabbis (Genesis Rabbah 55–56) identify the two places, and the Talmud says God saw the ashes of Isaac when he stopped the plague (Berakhot 62b). Most critical scholars think Genesis did not originally mean Jerusalem and that Chronicles made the link; the Samaritans placed Moriah at Mount Gerizim.

a: where he had shown himself to David
p: The Hebrew does not name a subject. The Greek supplies 'the Lord.'
b: The Hebrew says only asher nir'ah leDavid, "which appeared to David" or "where (he) appeared to David." It may mean the LORD appeared there (as the Greek, Rahlfs' edition, checked, reads: "where the Lord appeared to David"), or that the place "was shown" to David. In 1 Chronicles 21 it is the angel of the LORD whom David sees above the threshing floor, and the LORD answers with fire. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew's unnamed "he," which in context is the LORD. Either way the site was chosen by God, not by Solomon.

a: the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite
p: The Temple stands where David's plague was stopped. Samuel calls the owner Araunah; Chronicles, Ornan.
b: David bought the threshing floor, built an altar, and God answered with fire (1 Chronicles 21:18–22:1; 2 Samuel 24:18–25). David then declared it the site of "the house of the LORD God" (1 Chronicles 22:1). A threshing floor was a flat, open rock surface on high ground where the wind could carry off chaff. Most scholars place it on the hill north of the old City of David, the site of today's Temple Mount; many think it lay at or near the great rock now under the Dome of the Rock, though this cannot be proved.

a: in the fourth year of his reign
p: Kings dates the Temple from the exodus. Chronicles dates it only by Solomon's reign.
b: 1 Kings 6:1 says building began 480 years after Israel came out of Egypt, a number that anchors many datings of the exodus. Chronicles keeps the month and the year of Solomon's reign but drops the exodus date and the old month name Ziv. On the usual dates for Solomon (about 970–931 BC) the fourth year is about 966 BC. Chronicles ties its history to David and the Temple more than to the exodus; compare 6:11 and the end of the prayer (6:40–42).

a: by the old measure
p: There were two cubits: an older, longer one and a shorter common one. Chronicles says the Temple used the older one.
b: A cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, usually about 18 inches (45 centimeters). Egypt and later Israel also used a longer "royal" cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters). Ezekiel measures his Temple with "a cubit and a handbreadth" (Ezekiel 40:5; Ezekiel 43:13). By noting that Solomon used "the old measure," the writer tells readers of his own day that the Temple was larger than the numbers might suggest in their cubits. With the long cubit, 60 by 20 cubits is about 103 by 34 feet (31 by 10.4 meters). Chronicles leaves out the height of the house (30 cubits in 1 Kings 6:2).

a: a hundred and twenty cubits high
t: A porch as tall as a tower?
p: A porch 120 cubits high would be about 180 feet (55 meters), six times the height of the house.
b: Kings gives the porch no height and the house thirty cubits (1 Kings 6:2–3). A front tower of 120 cubits would make a strange building, though Herod's Temple did have a front about 100 cubits high, according to the Mishnah (Middot 4:6) and Josephus. Many scholars accept the reading "twenty" found in some Greek and Syriac copies, or think "hundred" crept in by a copying error. Others take the figure at face value or as a sign that Chronicles pictured the Temple in the grand style of later temples.

a: Parvaim gold
p: Parvaim is mentioned nowhere else. It was probably a gold-producing region, perhaps in Arabia.
b: The name appears only here. Suggestions include al-Farwain in Yemen, a place in eastern Arabia, or a general word for the far east. Like "gold of Ophir" (8:18), it seems to name a source of the finest gold. Chronicles also adds precious stones, matching the "onyx and gems to be set" and "every precious stone" that David had gathered (1 Chronicles 29:2).

a: six hundred talents
p: Six hundred talents is roughly 20 tons of gold, for one room.
b: A talent weighed about 75 pounds (34 kilograms), so six hundred talents is about 45,000 pounds or 20 metric tons. Compare the 666 talents Solomon took in each year (9:13) and the 100,000 talents David is said to have set aside (1 Chronicles 22:14). Some readers take the numbers literally, noting that ancient kings did cover temples in gold. Many scholars see the large numbers in Chronicles as a way of expressing the Temple's splendor rather than an inventory. Kings says only that the room was covered with "refined gold" (1 Kings 6:20).

a: a sculpted work
p: The word ts'atsu'im is found only here. Its meaning is a guess.
b: Ma'aseh ts'atsu'im is "a work of ts'atsu'im," a word used nowhere else. It may come from a root meaning "to shape" or "to carve," hence "sculpted" or "image work." The Greek translators wrote "a work of wood," perhaps guessing from 1 Kings 6:23, where the cherubim are of olive wood. Kings gives them a height of ten cubits; Chronicles gives only the wingspan.

a: with their faces turned toward the house
p: The cherubim on the ark faced each other. Solomon's great cherubim stood side by side, facing the hall.
b: On the atonement lid of the ark, "They will face each other, their faces turned toward the lid" (Exodus 25:20). Solomon's two giant cherubim stood on the floor of the most holy place, their wings spanning the room, and looked out toward the great hall. Many interpreters picture them as guardians of the throne, with the ark beneath their wings as God's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2). The cherubim of Eden guarded the way back to the tree of life (Genesis 3:24).

a: The curtain
p: Kings mentions doors for the inner room but no curtain. Chronicles has a curtain, like the tabernacle's veil.
b: The tabernacle had "a veil of violet, purple and scarlet yarn and twisted fine linen" with cherubim worked into it (Exodus 26:31). Kings describes olive-wood doors at the entrance to the inner room (1 Kings 6:31–32); Chronicles mentions doors too (4:22) but adds the curtain. Some scholars think Chronicles describes the Temple of its own day, which had a curtain, in the language of Exodus. Others think Solomon's Temple had both. The Gospels report that the curtain of Herod's Temple tore in two when Jesus died (Matthew 27:51; Mark 15:38), and Hebrews reads the curtain as a picture of Christ's flesh (Hebrews 10:20).

a: thirty-five cubits in length
t: How could the pillars be thirty-five cubits?
p: Kings and Jeremiah say each pillar was eighteen cubits tall. Chronicles says thirty-five.
b: 1 Kings 7:15 and Jeremiah 52:21 give eighteen cubits for each pillar. Several explanations are offered: (1) Chronicles gives the length of the two together, 36 cubits, rounded or less a cubit for the bases; (2) the figure counts the bronze as cast, before it was cut into two; (3) a copying error, since the Hebrew letters used for numbers 18 (yod-chet) and 35 (lamed-he) could be confused in some scripts. None is certain. The witnesses are given in the variant.

a: He made a bronze altar
p: Kings never describes the altar itself. This verse may have dropped out of Kings, or Chronicles may have added it.
b: The bronze altar was 20 by 20 cubits and 10 high, about 30 feet square and 15 feet tall (9 by 9 by 4.5 meters), far larger than the tabernacle's altar of 5 by 5 by 3 cubits (Exodus 27:1). Kings refers to it (1 Kings 8:64; 1 Kings 9:25) but has no verse describing its making. Some scholars think a sentence beginning "He made" dropped out of Kings, since the next verse also begins "He made" and a copyist's eye could skip between them. Others think Chronicles supplied it. An altar that high needed steps or a ramp; Ezekiel's altar has steps on the east (Ezekiel 43:13–17), though Exodus 20:26 forbade steps for the earlier altars.

a: The Sea, though, was where the priests washed.
t: What the basins and the Sea were for
p: Only Chronicles gives the purpose: the basins for rinsing the offerings, the Sea for the priests.
b: The tabernacle had one bronze basin for the priests to wash their hands and feet before serving (Exodus 30:17–21). Solomon's Temple had ten basins on wheeled stands and the great Sea. Kings describes them but never says how they were used. Chronicles explains: the basins were for rinsing the parts of the burnt offering, as Leviticus 1:9 and 1:13 require, and the Sea was for the priests' washing. The Sea, holding thousands of gallons, may also have stood as a symbol of the waters God tamed (see the note on 1 Kings 7:23).

a: ten of them
p: The tabernacle had one lampstand and one table. Solomon's Temple had ten of each.
b: Moses made one gold lampstand and one table for the bread (Exodus 25:23–40). Kings speaks of ten lampstands but of "the table" (1 Kings 7:48–49). Chronicles has ten tables as well (4:8; 4:19), as David's plan had "tables" (1 Chronicles 28:16). The Temple rebuilt after the exile seems to have had one lampstand and one table again: 1 Maccabees 1:21–22 and 4:49–51 tell how they were looted and remade, and the Arch of Titus in Rome shows one lampstand carried off in AD 70. "In the way they were meant to be made" means according to the pattern in Exodus.

a: the courtyard of the priests and the great enclosure
p: Chronicles distinguishes an inner court for the priests and a great outer court for the people.
b: Kings speaks of "the inner court" and "the great court" (1 Kings 6:36; 1 Kings 7:12). Chronicles names the inner one "the courtyard of the priests" and uses a late word, 'azarah, "enclosure," for the outer one. Elsewhere in the Bible it occurs only in 6:13 and in Ezekiel, where it means a ledge of the altar (Ezekiel 43:14; Ezekiel 45:19); later Hebrew used it for the Temple courts. The outer court's bronze-covered doors show its size. Chronicles places Solomon's platform (6:13) in this outer court.

a: Huram his father
p: The Hebrew calls the craftsman 'Huram his father' (Churam aviv). See the note on Huram-abi at 2:13.
b: The phrase Churam aviv is the same title as Churam avi in 2:13, with "his" in place of "my": the master craftsman of King Huram. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew so the reader sees the difference from 2:13.

a: between Succoth and Zeredah
p: Kings has Zarethan, Chronicles Zeredah. The bronze was cast in the clay of the Jordan valley.
b: 1 Kings 7:46 places the foundry "between Succoth and Zarethan." Chronicles writes Zeredah (Greek, checked: Sirdatha), probably the same place under a variant name, or an error for it. Succoth is usually placed at Tell Deir Alla, east of the Jordan, where excavations found evidence of metalworking. The valley's clay made good molds. See the note on 1 Kings 7:46.

a: the entrance of the house
p: Kings lists gold 'door sockets.' Chronicles has 'the entrance,' a word with nearly the same letters.
b: 1 Kings 7:50 ends the list with pothoth, the sockets or hinges for the doors, made of gold. Chronicles has pethach, "entrance," and then lists the doors themselves. The difference may be a copying change, or Chronicles may have rewritten an obscure word. Either way the doors to the most holy place and to the great hall were covered with gold.

a: the holy gifts of David his father
p: The silver, gold and objects David had dedicated from his wars and his own wealth go into the Temple treasury.
b: 1 Chronicles tells how David dedicated the spoils of his wars (1 Chronicles 18:8–11) and gave from his own treasure, with the leaders adding their gifts (1 Chronicles 29:1–9). Chronicles' picture is that David prepared and Solomon built: the two reigns form one project. Kings has the same verse (1 Kings 7:51), but in Chronicles it caps a much longer story of David's preparations.

a: at the feast. That is the seventh month.
p: The feast is the Feast of Booths. Kings names the month Ethanim; Chronicles drops the old name.
b: "The feast" of the seventh month is the Feast of Booths (Sukkot), the great autumn pilgrimage (Leviticus 23:33–43). Kings names the month by its old Canaanite name, Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2); Chronicles leaves it out, perhaps because its readers knew the month by the Babylonian name Tishri. The Hebrew reads awkwardly, "at the feast, that is the seventh month," as if a month name has fallen out. Kings says the Temple was finished in the eighth month of Solomon's eleventh year (1 Kings 6:38), so the dedication came either eleven months later or a month before it was finished.

a: the Levites picked up the ark
p: Kings says the priests carried the ark. Chronicles says the Levites, as David had ruled.
b: In 1 Kings 8:3 "the priests picked up the ark." Chronicles writes "the Levites," following David's rule: "The ark of God is not to be carried by anyone but the Levites" (1 Chronicles 15:2), which goes back to Deuteronomy 10:8 and Numbers 4:15. In 5:7, though, Chronicles keeps Kings' "the priests" for carrying the ark into the most holy place, where only priests could go. Many scholars see the Chronicler's concern that each group do its proper task. Since all priests were Levites, there is no contradiction for traditional readers.

a: showed from the ark
t: From the ark, or from the holy place?
p: Kings says the pole tips showed 'from the holy place.' Chronicles' Hebrew says 'from the ark.'
b: 1 Kings 8:8 has min-haqqodesh, "from the holy place"; Chronicles has min-ha'aron, "from the ark." The Greek of Chronicles (Rahlfs' edition, checked at blueletterbible.org) reads "from the holy place," as in Kings, and some Hebrew manuscripts are reported to do the same. "From the ark" may be a slip caught from "the ark" earlier in the verse; it can also be read as "extending from the ark." The Plain English Translation translates the Hebrew of Chronicles.

a: It has stayed there until today.
p: Chronicles copies this line from Kings, though the ark was gone by the time Chronicles was written.
b: Kings says the poles "have stayed there until today" (1 Kings 8:8). Chronicles keeps the phrase, though it was written long after Babylon burned the Temple in 586 BC. Many scholars take it as a phrase copied unchanged from the source. Some read it as the Chronicler's own hope, since Jewish tradition held that the ark was hidden, not destroyed (2 Maccabees 2:4–8; Bavli Yoma 53b). The Hebrew of Chronicles has a singular verb, "it has stayed," probably meaning the ark; Kings and the Greek have "they." See the variant and the note on 1 Kings 8:8.

a: whatever his division
p: David had divided the priests into twenty-four shifts. For the dedication, all of them served at once.
b: 1 Chronicles 24 describes twenty-four divisions of priests, each serving the Temple in turn for a week. At the dedication, Chronicles notes, the divisions were set aside: every priest who had made himself ritually clean took part. Chronicles adds 5:11b–13a to Kings, so that the cloud of glory comes at the moment the priests and Levites unite in praise. The same note returns at Hezekiah's Passover, when not enough priests had made themselves holy (30:3).

a: Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun
p: Chronicles adds the singers and musicians of David's organization to the dedication scene.
b: These three Levite families led the music David appointed (1 Chronicles 16:4–6, 16:37–42; 25:1–8). Their names stand over many psalms (Psalms 50 and 73–83 for Asaph; Psalm 88 for Heman the Ezrahite; Psalms 39, 62 and 77 mention Jeduthun). The "hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets" follow the Law, which gave trumpets to the priests (Numbers 10:8). Fine linen was a priestly fabric. The scene closely resembles the laying of the second Temple's foundation, when robed priests with trumpets and Levites of Asaph's family with cymbals praised the LORD (Ezra 3:10).
r: 1 Chronicles 15:16–24; 1 Chronicles 16:4–6; 1 Chronicles 16:37–42; 1 Chronicles 25:1–8; Numbers 10:8; Ezra 3:10–11

a: For he is good, for his loyal love is forever.
p: This line is the most-sung refrain of the Temple. It recurs throughout Chronicles, Ezra and the Psalms.
b: The words open Psalms 106, 107, 118 and 136 (where "for his loyal love is forever" ends every verse) and close David's psalm in 1 Chronicles 16:34. Chronicles uses the refrain at each high point of worship: here, at the fire from heaven (7:3, 7:6), and before Jehoshaphat's army (20:21). The returned exiles sang it when the second Temple's foundation was laid (Ezra 3:11), and Jeremiah promised it would be heard again in Jerusalem (Jeremiah 33:11). Its point is that God's covenant faithfulness outlasts everything, even exile.

a: Then the house was filled with a cloud
p: In Chronicles the cloud comes at the moment the singers and trumpeters praise together.
b: In Kings the cloud fills the house as soon as the priests leave the holy place (1 Kings 8:10). Chronicles inserts the music between the two events, so that the cloud comes when the trumpeters and singers become "as one" in praise. Many readers, Jewish and Christian, have drawn from this that God's presence is met in united worship; Psalm 22:3 pictures God seated as king on Israel's praises. Critical scholars see the Chronicler giving the Levite musicians of his own day a founding place in the Temple's first moment. The scene echoes the tabernacle: "The cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the LORD's glory filled the tabernacle" (Exodus 40:34).

a: Nor did I choose any man to be ruler over my people Israel.
p: Chronicles has two balanced choices: Jerusalem and David. The line about Jerusalem is missing from the Hebrew of Kings.
b: The full text sets two refusals against two choices: no city and no ruler before, but now Jerusalem and David. 1 Kings 8:16 has only the first refusal and the choice of David. Many scholars think Kings lost the middle words when a copyist's eye jumped from one "I chose" to another; the Greek of Kings and a small Qumran fragment seem to support a longer text (see the variant on 1 Kings 8:16). The double choice of Zion and David runs through Psalm 78:67–72 and Psalm 132:11–14, the psalm Solomon quotes at the end of this prayer (6:41–42).

a: the one he made with the Israelites
t: The exodus fades, David steps forward
p: Kings recalls the exodus here and at the end of the prayer. Chronicles drops both, and ends with David instead.
b: In 1 Kings 8:21 the covenant in the ark is the one God made "with our ancestors when he brought them out from the land of Egypt." Chronicles has simply "with the Israelites." Kings ends the prayer by recalling the iron furnace of Egypt and Moses (1 Kings 8:51–53); Chronicles ends with Psalm 132 and God's loyal love to David (6:41–42). Scholars (Japhet, Williamson) see a shift of weight: Israel's foundation story, for Chronicles, is less the exodus than God's choice of David and Jerusalem. Chronicles still mentions the exodus (5:10; 6:5; 7:22), so it is a change of emphasis, not a denial.

a: a bronze platform
p: Only Chronicles mentions the platform. The word usually means a basin.
b: Kiyyor is the word used for the basins in 4:6, here a round or square stand, 5 by 5 by 3 cubits (about 7.5 by 7.5 by 4.5 feet, or 2.3 by 2.3 by 1.4 meters), set in the outer court. It let the crowd see the king, and it kept him out of the priests' court, near the altar but not at it. Kings has Solomon stand "before the LORD's altar" and later rise from his knees (1 Kings 8:22, 8:54). Some scholars think this verse fell out of Kings by a copyist's slip, since it ends with the same words as the verse before ("spread out his palms"); others think the Chronicler added it to explain how Solomon could both stand and kneel. Royal platforms are known from Assyrian reliefs, and kings stand "by the pillar" in 23:13 and 2 Kings 11:14.

a: walk in my law
p: Where Kings says 'walk before me,' Chronicles says 'walk in my law': faithfulness is measured by the Torah.
b: 1 Kings 8:25 has "walk before me as you walked before me." Chronicles changes the first phrase to "walk in my law" (torati). Torah means "instruction, teaching" as well as "law"; in Chronicles it usually means the written Law of Moses, which the good kings keep and teach (17:9; 31:21; 34:14). For readers after the exile, who no longer had a king, the condition laid on David's sons was something every Israelite could keep.

a: with human beings
p: Chronicles adds 'with human beings' to Kings' question: can God really live on earth?
b: Kings asks, "can God truly make his home on earth?" (1 Kings 8:27). Chronicles adds et ha'adam, "with humankind." The question becomes not only whether a building can hold God, but whether God would live among people at all. The Greek translators made it "with human beings on the earth." Christians have long read this question beside John 1:14, "the Word became flesh and lived among us" (fresh rendering), and Revelation 21:3.

a: Pay back the guilty man
p: Kings has 'declare the guilty man guilty.' Chronicles has 'pay back,' a slightly different verb.
b: In 1 Kings 8:32 God is asked leharshia' rasha', "to declare the guilty guilty." Chronicles has lehashiv larasha', "to return to the guilty," that is, to repay him. The difference is small in Hebrew letters and may be a copying change, or Chronicles may prefer the idea of repayment, which suits its interest in each person reaping what they sow. See the note on 1 Kings 8:31 about oaths at the altar.

a: his own wound and his own pain
p: Kings speaks of the 'wound in his own heart.' Chronicles has 'his own wound and his own pain.'
b: 1 Kings 8:38 has nega' levavo, "the wound in his own heart," which can mean grief, guilt or both. Chronicles has nig'o umakh'ovo, "his blow and his pain," which points more to the disaster itself, the plague or famine just listed. Either way the prayer asks God to hear each person in their own suffering.

a: as prisoners to a land far away or near
p: For Chronicles' readers, many still scattered, this part of the prayer described their own world.
b: When Chronicles was written, Jews lived in Babylon, Persia and Egypt as well as Judah. Solomon's prayer asked that captives who turned back and prayed toward the land, the city and the house would be heard (6:37–39). Daniel prays toward Jerusalem from Babylon (Daniel 6:10), and Nehemiah's prayer echoes this one (Nehemiah 1:5–11). Jewish prayer still faces Jerusalem, a custom the Talmud bases on this chapter (Bavli Berakhot 30a). See the notes on 1 Kings 8:29 and 1 Kings 8:46–47.

a: let your ears pay attention to prayer from this place
p: Chronicles' own close to the prayer. God answers in the same words (7:15), and Nehemiah prays them.
b: Kings ends the prayer differently (1 Kings 8:51–53). Chronicles' line about God's eyes and ears is answered almost word for word in 7:15, "Now my eyes will be open, and my ears will pay attention to prayer from this place." Nehemiah, a generation or more before Chronicles was finished, uses the same pair: "may your ear listen closely and your eyes be open" (Nehemiah 1:6, fresh rendering; compare Nehemiah 1:11). Psalm 130:2 asks the same.

a: up, LORD God, to your place of rest
p: The prayer ends with lines from Psalm 132:8–10, a song of the ark going up to Zion.
b: Psalm 132 remembers David's oath to find a home for the ark and God's oath to David. Its lines run: "Up, LORD, to your place of rest, you and the ark of your strength! May your priests wear righteousness like clothes, and your faithful ones shout for joy. For the sake of David your servant, do not turn your anointed one away" (Psalm 132:8–10). Chronicles adds "LORD God" twice, has "salvation" for "righteousness" (as in Psalm 132:16), and "be glad in good things" for "shout for joy." The cry "Up, LORD" (Hebrew qumah, "rise up") goes back to Moses' words when the ark set out, "Rise up, LORD!" (Numbers 10:35). Now the ark arrives at rest.

a: your place of rest
p: The ark's resting place fulfills God's promise of rest to David's son, 'a man of rest.'
b: The word nuach, "rest," ties the prayer to the promise in 1 Chronicles 22:9: "He will be a man of rest. From the enemies all around him I will give him rest." David had set his heart on "building a resting house for the ark of the LORD's covenant" (1 Chronicles 28:2). Rest in the land, rest for the king, and rest for the ark come together in the Temple. Hebrews takes up the theme and says a greater rest still remains (Hebrews 4:8–9).

a: your anointed one
p: Meshiach means 'anointed one,' the king. The same word later gave us 'Messiah.'
b: Kings in Israel were anointed with oil when they took the throne (1 Kings 1:39), so "the LORD's anointed" was the reigning king, here Solomon himself. After the exile, with no king on the throne, Jewish hope looked for a future anointed son of David, "the Messiah" (from Hebrew mashiach; Greek Christos). Psalm 132 and this prayer were read in that light. The Leningrad Codex reads the plural, "your anointed ones" (perhaps David and Solomon); the Plain English Translation follows the singular, as in Psalm 132:10. See the variant.

a: the loyal love shown to David your servant
p: The Hebrew 'David's loyal loves' can mean God's loyal love to David, or David's own loyal deeds.
b: Chasdei David is literally "the loyal loves of David." Most readers take it as God's promises of loyal love to David, as in Isaiah 55:3, "the sure loyal love promised to David" (fresh rendering), quoted in Acts 13:34. Others note that Chronicles uses the plural chasadim for a king's own good deeds (32:32; 35:26), and read it as "remember David's faithful deeds," as Psalm 132:1 asks God to remember David's hardships. Both fit the psalm.

a: fire came down out of the heavens
p: As at the tabernacle and at David's altar, God accepts the new altar with fire from heaven.
b: Kings has no fire here. Chronicles places the Temple in a line of divine approvals: at the first sacrifices of the tabernacle, "Fire came out from before the LORD and ate up the burnt offering" (Leviticus 9:24); at David's altar on this very site, "fire came from heaven onto the altar of burnt offering" (1 Chronicles 21:26); and later at Elijah's altar on Mount Carmel (1 Kings 18:38). Jewish tradition held that this fire was kept burning on the altar until the exile (compare Leviticus 6:13; 2 Maccabees 1:18–36).

a: the LORD's glory filled the LORD's house
p: The cloud of glory fills the house in 5:13–14 and again here. Readers explain the repetition differently.
b: Chronicles copies the cloud scene from Kings (5:13–14; 1 Kings 8:10–11) and then adds a second filling after the prayer. Some read two moments: the glory filled the house when the ark arrived, and fire and glory answered the prayer. Others see a literary frame around Solomon's prayer, so that the prayer stands inside the glory. Critical scholars often see Chronicles combining its Kings source with its own addition. In both places the priests cannot enter, just as Moses could not enter the tent (Exodus 40:35).

a: when David gave praise through them
t: David's praise in the Levites' hands
p: The Hebrew 'when David praised by their hand' means the Levites performed the praise David composed or ordered.
b: Behallel David beyadam is "in David's praising by their hand." Most take it to mean that the Levites sang the songs and used the instruments David had provided (1 Chronicles 23:5), so David's praise went on through them. Chronicles treats David as the founder of Temple music, much as Moses founded the sacrifices (8:14; 29:25–30; 35:15). The Psalms' many headings "of David" fit this tradition.

a: for seven days
p: Chronicles spells out the fourteen days of Kings: a week for the altar, then the week of the Feast of Booths.
b: 1 Kings 8:65–66 speaks of "seven days and then seven days more" and sends the people home on "the eighth day." Chronicles clarifies: the altar's dedication took seven days, then the Feast of Booths seven days (the 15th to the 21st of the seventh month), then the closing gathering on the eighth day (the 22nd), as the Law requires: "On the eighth day hold a holy gathering ... It is the closing assembly" (Leviticus 23:36). The people went home on the 23rd. The dedication week would have included the Day of Atonement on the 10th. The Talmud discusses this and says the people did not fast that year (Bavli Mo'ed Katan 9a).

a: for David and for Solomon
p: Kings says the people rejoiced over God's goodness to David. Chronicles adds Solomon.
b: 1 Kings 8:66 has "all the good the LORD had done for David his servant and for Israel his people." Chronicles adds "and for Solomon." It is a small change that fits a large pattern: in Chronicles David and Solomon are paired as joint founders of the Temple (11:17; 35:4). Scholars such as Braun and Williamson describe the two as a single, ideal reign in Chronicles' telling.

a: to be a house of sacrifice
t: A house of sacrifice and of prayer
p: God's answer adds that he has chosen the Temple as a house of sacrifice. Isaiah calls it a house of prayer.
b: Kings' version of God's answer begins with the prayer and the house (1 Kings 9:3). Chronicles adds that God has chosen this place as beit zavach, "a house of sacrifice," the only time the phrase occurs. It confirms the altar and its worship. Isaiah gives the other side: God's house will be called "a house of prayer for all the peoples" (Isaiah 56:7, fresh rendering), which Jesus quoted in the Temple (Mark 11:17). Solomon's prayer has already made the house a place to pray toward (6:20–40).

a: and my people, over whom my name has been called, humble themselves
p: This verse is quoted far beyond its setting, especially in America. Readers differ on how widely it applies.
b: In context God answers Solomon's prayer about drought, locusts and disease (6:26–31): if Israel, the people who bear his name, turn back, he will forgive them and heal their land. Jewish readers see a promise to Israel tied to the land and the Temple, and a pattern for repentance on fast days. Many Christians, especially in the United States, apply it to a nation's or the church's revival and pray it at national prayer gatherings. Others caution that "my people" and "their land" mean Israel, while granting that the call to humility, prayer and turning back fits any of God's people (compare James 4:10). The four verbs, humble, pray, seek, turn, describe repentance in Chronicles, and the rest of the book shows them at work (12:6–7; 33:12–13).

a: humble themselves
p: Kana', 'humble oneself,' is a key word in Chronicles. Kings uses it only rarely.
b: The verb nikhna', "to bend low, humble oneself," appears here first and then marks the turning points of 2 Chronicles: Rehoboam and his leaders humble themselves and are spared (12:6–12); Hezekiah humbles himself (32:26); Manasseh, the worst king, humbles himself in exile and is restored (33:12–13; 33:19); Josiah humbles himself when he hears the Law (34:27); and the last king, Zedekiah, "did not humble himself" (36:12). Kings uses the word of Ahab (1 Kings 21:29) and of Josiah (2 Kings 22:19).

a: ruling over Israel
p: Kings says 'from Israel's throne.' Chronicles says 'from ruling over Israel,' words that recall Micah's promise.
b: 1 Kings 9:5 promises that a man of David's will never be cut off "from Israel's throne." Chronicles has moshel beYisra'el, "one ruling in Israel," and calls the promise a covenant. The phrase is close to Micah 5:2, where a ruler in Israel will come from Bethlehem (Micah 5:1 in Hebrew), a verse Matthew applies to Jesus (Matthew 2:6). H. G. M. Williamson argued that the change shows Chronicles still expected a future king of David's line; others think it means no more than "king."

a: I will pull them up by the roots
p: The verb natash, 'uproot,' is the language of exile in Deuteronomy and Jeremiah.
b: Kings has "I will cut Israel off" (1 Kings 9:7). Chronicles has natash, "pull up by the roots," the verb of Deuteronomy 29:28, where "the LORD pulled them up by the roots from their own soil", and of Jeremiah's call "to pull up and pull down, to destroy and demolish, to build and to plant" (Jeremiah 1:10, fresh rendering). For readers after the exile, this warning had already happened (36:17–20), and its other half, to build and to plant, was what they hoped for.

a: I will throw away out of my sight
p: Chronicles has 'I will throw' (ashlikh). Kings has 'I will send away' (ashallach).
b: 1 Kings 9:7 has ashallach, "I will send away," which the site's Kings page renders "throw away" for sense. Chronicles has ashlikh, "I will throw," a stronger and more common verb for rejection (compare 2 Kings 17:20). The English of the two pages is the same, but the Hebrew words differ.

a: which was so high
p: Kings says 'this house will be high.' Chronicles says it 'was high,' looking back at a ruin.
b: 1 Kings 9:8 has yihyeh 'elyon, "will be high," a famous difficulty; many scholars emend Kings to "will become a heap of ruins" with the Syriac and Old Latin. Chronicles has asher hayah 'elyon, "which was high," which reads naturally: everyone who passes the house that once stood so high will be stunned. Chronicles' wording may be an early attempt to smooth the difficulty in Kings, or a different text. For its readers the house had in fact been destroyed (36:19).
orig: אֲשֶׁר הָיָה עֶלְיוֹן (asher hayah 'elyon), 'which was high'

a: the towns Huram had given to Solomon
p: Kings says Solomon gave Hiram twenty towns. Chronicles says Hiram gave towns to Solomon.
b: See the note on 1 Kings 9:11, which sets out the readings. In short: harmonizers say Hiram, displeased with the towns (1 Kings 9:12–13), handed them back, and Solomon rebuilt and settled them; many critical scholars think Chronicles changed a story in which Solomon paid a foreign king with part of the promised land. Chronicles also leaves out Hiram's 120 talents of gold (1 Kings 9:14) and Hiram's complaint.

a: Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and overpowered it
p: This is the one military campaign Chronicles gives Solomon, the 'man of rest.' Kings has none.
b: Hamath was a kingdom on the Orontes River in Syria; Zobah, an Aramean state David defeated (1 Chronicles 18:3–9). "Hamath-zobah" may be one region or a combined name. Kings gives Solomon no wars, and in Chronicles his reign is otherwise one of peace, as promised (1 Chronicles 22:9). Some scholars think the Chronicler read Kings' "Tamar in the wilderness" as Tadmor (8:4) and filled in a campaign to reach it; others think he had an independent source. There is no outside evidence either way.

a: Tadmor in the wilderness
p: Tadmor is Palmyra, the famous oasis city in the Syrian desert. Kings' written text has Tamar, a town in the south.
b: 1 Kings 9:18 reads Tamar in its written Hebrew (Ketiv), probably a town in the Judean wilderness south of the Dead Sea (Ezekiel 47:19). Its reading tradition (Qere) and Chronicles read Tadmor, the oasis about 130 miles (210 kilometers) northeast of Damascus, later the Roman city of Palmyra. Traditional readers accept that Solomon's power reached that far, as 9:26 claims. Most critical scholars think Tadmor here reflects later geography and doubt that a 10th-century king of Jerusalem held it. Josephus, following Chronicles, says Solomon founded Palmyra (Antiquities 8.154).

a: Upper Beth-horon and Lower Beth-horon
p: The two Beth-horons guarded the main pass from the coast up to Jerusalem.
b: Upper and Lower Beth-horon (modern Beit Ur al-Foqa and Beit Ur al-Tahta) sat on a ridge road that climbs from the Aijalon valley to the hills north of Jerusalem. Joshua chased the Amorite kings down this road (Joshua 10:10–11), and Judas Maccabeus fought there (1 Maccabees 3:16–24). Later the Syrian general Bacchides fortified Beth-horon again, "with high walls and gates and bars" (1 Maccabees 9:50). Kings lists Lower Beth-horon with Gezer (1 Kings 9:17); Chronicles leaves out Gezer and the story of Pharaoh's capturing it as a dowry for his daughter (1 Kings 9:16), and also the Millo, Hazor and Megiddo (1 Kings 9:15).

a: As for Pharaoh's daughter
p: Chronicles mentions Pharaoh's daughter only here, and only to keep her away from the holy places.
b: Kings names Pharaoh's daughter five times, first as the start of Solomon's foreign marriages (1 Kings 3:1) and last among the wives who turned his heart (1 Kings 11:1). Chronicles drops all but this verse and gives a reason Kings does not: a place where the ark had been was holy. Many readers take this as Solomon's own care for holiness: a foreign wife, or any woman (compare the rules of ritual purity in Leviticus 15), should not live in rooms the ark had made holy. Others hear a quiet admission of the problem Kings makes plain, that his marriages did not fit God's house (compare Nehemiah 13:26). Rabbinic tradition also discussed this marriage as the beginning of Solomon's troubles.
r: 1 Kings 3:1; 1 Kings 7:8; 1 Kings 9:24; 1 Kings 11:1; Nehemiah 13:26; Deuteronomy 17:17

a: three times a year
p: Solomon keeps the daily offerings and the three yearly feasts the Law commands.
b: Kings sums it up in one line (1 Kings 9:25). Chronicles spells out the calendar: daily offerings, Sabbaths, new moons, and the three pilgrim feasts of Deuteronomy 16:16, Unleavened Bread (with Passover, in spring), Weeks (Shavuot, early summer) and Booths (Sukkot, autumn). The list echoes Solomon's letter (2:4) and the offerings of Numbers 28–29. Hezekiah and Josiah will restore the same pattern (31:3; 35:1–19).

a: David the man of God
p: Only Chronicles and Nehemiah call David 'the man of God,' a title usually given to prophets.
b: "Man of God" is used for Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel, Elijah, Elisha and other prophets. Chronicles and Nehemiah give it to David (Nehemiah 12:24; Nehemiah 12:36) because he gave inspired commands for worship, just as Moses did for the sacrifices. The divisions of priests, Levites and gatekeepers come from 1 Chronicles 23–26. In Chronicles' view the Temple's order rests on two founders: Moses (8:13) and David (8:14).

a: The LORD's house was complete.
p: The word for 'complete' sounds like Solomon's name.
b: Shalem, "complete, whole," shares its root with Shelomoh, Solomon, and with shalom, "peace." The man of peace (1 Chronicles 22:9) completes the house. Chronicles closes the building story with this line, as Kings closes it with "So he brought the house to completion" (1 Kings 9:25), using the same root.

a: Huram sent him ships
p: How could Hiram of Tyre send ships to the Red Sea? Kings says Solomon built them there.
b: Kings says Solomon built the fleet at Ezion-geber and Hiram sent sailors (1 Kings 9:26–27). Chronicles says Hiram "sent him ships." Some think the ships were carried overland in sections, as ancient fleets sometimes were; others that "ships" means materials and shipwrights; others that Chronicles simply means Hiram supplied the fleet. Ezion-geber and Eloth lay at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba; Chronicles drops Kings' "Sea of Reeds" (1 Kings 9:26). On Ophir see the note on 1 Kings 9:28; on the number of talents, see the variant.

a: The queen of Sheba heard the news about Solomon.
p: Jesus held up the queen of Sheba as a seeker of wisdom. Kings adds that her news was tied to the LORD's name.
b: Chronicles copies 1 Kings 10:1–13 closely but drops the phrase "news tied to the name of the LORD" (1 Kings 10:1). Jesus told his hearers that "the queen of the South" would rise at the judgment and condemn them, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon's wisdom, "and look, more than Solomon is here" (Matthew 12:42, fresh rendering; Luke 11:31). On Sheba, the incense trade, and Ethiopian tradition, see the notes on 1 Kings 10.

a: seated you on his own throne, as king for the LORD your God
p: Kings says God seated Solomon 'on Israel's throne.' Chronicles says 'on his own throne': the kingdom is God's.
b: 1 Kings 10:9 has "on Israel's throne." Chronicles has "on his throne" and adds "as king for the LORD your God." This fits a theme of Chronicles: the kingdom belongs to God, and David's sons sit on it in his place. God promised to set David's son "in my house and in my kingdom" (1 Chronicles 17:14), and "Solomon sat on the LORD's throne as king in place of David his father" (1 Chronicles 29:23). Abijah will tell the north that it is fighting the LORD's own kingdom, held by David's sons (13:8).

a: steps
p: Kings says the king made 'supports' from the wood; Chronicles, 'steps' or 'paths.' Both words are uncertain.
b: 1 Kings 10:12 has mis'ad, "support" or "railing." Chronicles has mesillot, which usually means raised roads or paths, perhaps steps or terraces. The Greek of Chronicles (Rahlfs' edition, checked) has "ascents." Chronicles also changes Kings' remark that no such wood has come "to this day" into "nothing like them had been seen before in the land of Judah," naming the kingdom of its own day.

a: besides what she had brought to the king
p: Kings says Solomon gave her gifts besides what she asked for. Chronicles says he gave more than she had brought.
b: Kings: Solomon gave her all she asked, "on top of the gifts he gave her with a king's open hand" (1 Kings 10:13). Chronicles: "besides what she had brought to the king." It may mean Solomon gave her back gifts worth more than hers, as royal etiquette required, or that he gave her what she asked in addition to returning the value of her gifts. Either way, Solomon outgives his guest.
orig: מִלְּבַד אֲשֶׁר־הֵבִיאָה אֶל־הַמֶּלֶךְ (millevad asher hevi'ah el hammelekh)

a: three hundred shekels of gold
t: Three hundred shekels or three minas?
p: Kings has three minas of gold per shield; Chronicles three hundred shekels.
b: A mina was 50 shekels (or 60 in some systems), so three minas would be 150 or 180 shekels, not 300. Chronicles may reckon in a different unit, or the word "shekels" may be supplied wrongly by translators, since the Hebrew has only "three hundred of gold." A shekel was about 0.4 ounce (11.4 grams). Shishak will take these shields (12:9).

a: a footstool of gold
p: Chronicles mentions a gold footstool fastened to the throne. Kings has a round top or a calf's head instead.
b: Footstools were part of royal thrones in the ancient world; one of gold and ebony was found in Tutankhamun's tomb. In the Bible the ark is "the footstool of our God's feet" (1 Chronicles 28:2), and the earth is God's footstool (Isaiah 66:1; Matthew 5:35). Kings has something else at the same place in the sentence (1 Kings 10:19); see the variant.

a: ships going to Tarshish
p: Kings speaks of 'Tarshish ships,' a type of large ship. Chronicles says the ships went to Tarshish.
b: "Tarshish ships" were big seagoing merchant ships, named after the far western port (see the note on 1 Kings 10:22). These sailed from the Red Sea (8:17–18), so they could not have reached Tarshish in Spain without going around Africa. Chronicles (and its Greek, checked) has "ships going to Tarshish," and does the same in 20:36. Most scholars think the Chronicler took the type name as a destination. Some suggest a different Tarshish in the east, or a voyage around Africa, which the three-year round trip might fit.

a: four thousand stalls
p: Chronicles' 4,000 stalls fits Solomon's 1,400 chariots far better than Kings' 40,000.
b: 1 Kings 4:26 has forty thousand stalls. Chronicles' four thousand is the likelier figure for 1,400 chariots (1:14), allowing two or three horses a chariot with spares. Excavations at Megiddo uncovered long pillared buildings once called "Solomon's stables"; most archaeologists now date them to the 9th or 8th century BC, and some think they were storehouses. See the variant on 1 Kings 4:26.

a: and out of all the lands
p: Chronicles drops Kings' Que and the export trade, already used at 1:16–17, and says the horses came from all lands.
b: 1 Kings 10:28–29 names Egypt and Que and gives prices for chariots and horses. Chronicles has already copied that at 1:16–17, so here it gives only a summary and widens it: horses came "out of all the lands." The change fits 9:23–24, where all the kings of the earth bring Solomon gifts.

a: The rest of Solomon's story
p: Chronicles ends Solomon's reign without his foreign wives, his idols or God's anger in 1 Kings 11. Why?
b: In Kings, Solomon's wives turn his heart to other gods, God raises enemies against him, and the kingdom is torn away for his sin (1 Kings 11:1–40). Chronicles goes from Solomon's glory straight to his death. (1) It assumes Kings. Its readers knew the story; Nehemiah 13:26 recalls Solomon's sin by name. Chronicles even mentions Ahijah's prophecy without telling it (10:15). (2) An ideal portrait. Japhet, Braun and Williamson see David and Solomon as the model reign around the Temple, the pattern for the future. (3) The book's logic of blessing. In Chronicles sin is usually punished in the sinner's own lifetime; Solomon's reign ends in peace, so the writer passes over the sins. (4) Jewish tradition debated Solomon's guilt; one Talmudic saying holds that whoever says Solomon sinned is mistaken, reading 1 Kings 11 as about failing to stop his wives (Bavli Shabbat 56b). The silence is not denial, but a choice of focus.

a: the accounts of Nathan the prophet, in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the visionary
p: Kings cites 'the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds.' Chronicles cites three prophets.
b: 1 Kings 11:41 refers readers to "the Scroll of Solomon's Deeds." Chronicles names the records of Nathan, who spoke the promise to David; Ahijah, who foretold the split (1 Kings 11:29–39); and Iddo, otherwise unknown except in 12:15 and 13:22. Traditional readers take these as real prophetic writings, now lost, and see in them the Jewish view that the history books were written by prophets (the "Former Prophets"). Many critical scholars think they are sections of Samuel–Kings named after the prophets who appear in them, or the Chronicler's way of saying the history carries a prophet's authority.

a: Rehoboam went to Shechem.
p: Chronicles leaves out almost everything about the northern kingdom, but it tells the split in full.
b: From here on Chronicles follows only the kings of Judah. It mentions northern kings only when they meet Judah. Yet it copies the story of the split almost word for word from 1 Kings 12:1–19, because it is Judah's story too: the son of David loses most of Israel. It then leaves out Jeroboam's crowning and his golden calves (1 Kings 12:20–33), which it mentions only in passing (11:15; 13:8–9). Shechem was the old center of the northern tribes (Joshua 24:1); see the note on 1 Kings 12:1.

a: When Jeroboam son of Nebat heard of it
p: Chronicles has never mentioned Jeroboam's rebellion, Ahijah's prophecy or his flight to Egypt.
b: In Kings, Jeroboam was one of Solomon's officials; the prophet Ahijah tore a new cloak into twelve pieces and gave him ten (1 Kings 11:26–40); Solomon tried to kill him, and he fled to Shishak in Egypt. Chronicles left all that out with the rest of 1 Kings 11, yet here and in 10:15 it takes it for granted. This is one of the clearest signs that Chronicles was written for readers who already knew Kings. The verbs "came back" and "was living" differ only in their vowels, and the prepositions "from" and "in" differ too; see the variant.

a: Be kind to this people
p: In Kings the elders tell Rehoboam to be the people's servant. In Chronicles, to be kind to them.
b: Kings: "If you become a servant to this people today and serve them ... they will be your servants for all time" (1 Kings 12:7). Chronicles: "Be kind to this people, show them favor." Some scholars think Chronicles found the idea of a king serving his subjects too strong and toned it down. Others see no change of meaning, only of words: the Greek of Chronicles (checked) keeps "today" from Kings, which suggests a closely related text. Both versions keep the elders' point: gentle words would have kept the kingdom.

a: God had brought about this turn
t: God's plan and a king's folly
p: Chronicles keeps Kings' surprising statement that God was behind Rehoboam's foolish answer.
b: The word nesibbah, "a turn of events," comes from God. The text holds two causes together: Rehoboam chose badly, and God used his choice to keep the word spoken through Ahijah (1 Kings 11:29–39). Chronicles keeps this, though it never told Ahijah's prophecy (see 10:2). Readers compare Joseph's words, "You planned evil against me, but God planned it for good" (Genesis 50:20), and 1 Chronicles 10:14, where Saul dies for his own sin and "the LORD" turns the kingdom to David. Jewish and Christian interpreters have used this verse in discussing how God's purposes and human freedom fit together.

a: Hadoram
p: The same official has three forms of his name.
b: Solomon's officer over forced labor is Adoniram in 1 Kings 4:6 and 1 Kings 5:14, Adoram in 1 Kings 12:18 and 2 Samuel 20:24, and Hadoram here. The Greek of Chronicles (checked) has Adoniram. Sending the man in charge of the hated labor gangs to calm a revolt against them was a final blunder. If he is the same Adoram who served David (2 Samuel 20:24), he was by now an old man.

a: and so it stands to this day
p: Kings wrote this while the northern kingdom stood. Chronicles keeps it centuries after Israel's fall.
b: The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17). Chronicles was written long after, yet keeps the phrase. In its own day the division still mattered: the people of the old northern territory, among them the community that became the Samaritans, worshiped apart from Jerusalem. Yet Chronicles also speaks warmly of northerners who came to Jerusalem (11:16; 30:11, 30:18), and calls the whole people "all Israel." Scholars such as Williamson read this as an open door: the split was real, but the Temple was still the place where all Israel could be one.

a: all Israel in Judah and Benjamin
p: Kings says 'all the house of Judah and Benjamin.' Chronicles calls the southern people 'all Israel.'
b: In 1 Kings 12:23 the word goes to "all the house of Judah and Benjamin, and to the rest of the people." Chronicles has "all Israel in Judah and Benjamin." For Chronicles, "Israel" is not only the northern kingdom: the people loyal to David's house and the Temple are Israel (10:17; 12:1; 12:6). This mattered for the small community after the exile, which saw itself as the heir of all twelve tribes (1 Chronicles 9:3). Yet the north is still "your kinsmen" (11:4), not enemies.

a: He built up towns in Judah to defend it.
p: The fifteen towns ring Judah on the south and west, not the north. Scholars debate their date.
b: The list (11:6–10) runs from Bethlehem and Tekoa south to Hebron and Ziph, and west to Lachish, Azekah and Aijalon. No forts face the northern kingdom. Many scholars link the line to Shishak's invasion: Rehoboam built it after Egypt's attack, or in fear of it, though Chronicles places it before (12:4). Others, such as Nadav Na'aman, think the list fits the time of Hezekiah, about 700 BC, many of whose stamped jar handles come from these towns. Excavations at Lachish and other sites show building in the 10th and 9th centuries, but cannot tie it to Rehoboam by name.

a: Gath
p: Gath was a Philistine city. Its place in a list of Judah's forts is puzzling.
b: Gath was one of the five Philistine cities, Goliath's hometown (1 Samuel 17:4), usually identified with Tell es-Safi. David had taken it (1 Chronicles 18:1). Some think Judah held it in Rehoboam's day; others that this is a different Gath, such as Moresheth-gath, the town of the prophet Micah (Micah 1:14), which would fit the list better.

a: The Levites had left behind their pasturelands
p: Kings says Jeroboam made priests from anyone. Chronicles adds that the true priests and Levites left for Judah.
b: 1 Kings 12:31 says Jeroboam "made priests out of the general run of the people, men who were not from the sons of Levi." Chronicles draws the consequence: the Levites lost their place in the north and left their towns and land (1 Chronicles 6:54–81) to go to Jerusalem, and devout people from every tribe followed (11:16). Critical scholars see the Chronicler's conviction that legitimate worship belongs in Jerusalem; some also see a real movement of people south after the split, which archaeology may reflect in Jerusalem's growth, though most date that growth to after 722 BC.

a: the goat idols
p: The Hebrew se'irim means 'goats.' Here, as in Leviticus 17:7, it means goat-shaped idols or demons.
b: Leviticus forbids sacrifice "to the goat idols, which they go after" (Leviticus 17:7). Se'irim may be idols in goat form, or demons imagined as hairy goats living in waste places (Isaiah 13:21; Isaiah 34:14). Kings mentions only the calves (1 Kings 12:28). The Greek of Chronicles (Rahlfs' edition, checked) has "idols and vain things and calves." Pairing the calves with goat idols puts Jeroboam's worship in the worst light.

a: made up their minds to seek the LORD
p: To 'seek' the LORD is Chronicles' word for true faith. It uses two verbs for it, darash and biqqesh.
b: The Hebrew is "those who gave their heart to seek the LORD." Here the verb is biqqesh, as in 7:14, "seeking my face." Chronicles more often uses darash (1:5; 12:14), over forty times, for turning to God in worship, prayer and obedience; the two verbs mean much the same. Seeking the LORD brings blessing: David told Solomon, "Seek him, and he will let you find him" (1 Chronicles 28:9), and a prophet will say the same to Asa (15:2). Not seeking him is the root of failure, as with Saul (1 Chronicles 10:14) and Rehoboam (12:14).

a: Mahalath, daughter of Jerimoth son of David
p: Rehoboam married within David's family. Jerimoth is not in the lists of David's sons.
b: Jerimoth does not appear among David's named sons (1 Chronicles 3:1–9), so he may have been a son of a concubine: "These were all David's sons, apart from the concubines' sons" (1 Chronicles 3:9). Abihail is either Mahalath's mother or a second wife; the Greek (checked) seems to take her as another wife. Eliab was David's eldest brother (1 Samuel 16:6). Both of Rehoboam's named wives were from David's family: Mahalath through David's son and brother, Maacah through Absalom (11:20). His mother was an Ammonite (12:13).

a: Maacah daughter of Absalom
p: 13:2 calls Abijah's mother Micaiah daughter of Uriel. Many think 'daughter' here means 'granddaughter.'
b: 1 Kings 15:2 calls Abijam's mother "Maacah, Abishalom's daughter." 2 Chronicles 13:2 calls her "Micaiah daughter of Uriel of Gibeah." David's son Absalom had one daughter, Tamar (2 Samuel 14:27). Josephus makes Maacah the daughter of Absalom's daughter Tamar, so Absalom's granddaughter (Antiquities 8.249); combined with 13:2, her father would be Uriel. Hebrew "daughter" can mean any female descendant. Others think Abishalom was a different man. The name Micaiah in 13:2 is probably a variant of Maacah.

a: eighteen wives and sixty concubines
p: Rehoboam's harem is smaller than his father's, but Chronicles reports it without comment.
b: Of Solomon, 1 Kings 11:3 says: "Seven hundred wives belonged to him, women of noble rank, and three hundred concubines." Deuteronomy 17:17 warns, "He must not take many wives for himself, or his heart will turn aside." Chronicles lists Rehoboam's wives and children, as it does Abijah's (13:21), among the signs of a king's strength. Many children were a mark of blessing in the ancient world (Psalm 127:3–5), and royal marriages were alliances. Modern readers note that the Bible describes polygamy among kings without endorsing it, and that its stories often show the trouble it brought.
r: 1 Kings 11:3; Deuteronomy 17:17; 13:21; Psalm 127:3–5; Song of Songs 6:8

a: for he meant to make him king
p: Rehoboam chose the son of his favorite wife over older brothers, the very thing Deuteronomy forbids for inheritance.
b: Abijah was not the firstborn: Mahalath's sons came first (11:19–20). Deuteronomy 21:15–17 deals with a man who has "two wives, one loved and the other unloved": he "may not treat the son of the loved wife as firstborn ahead of the son of the unloved wife, who is the real firstborn." Chronicles does not comment, but the echo of "loved" (11:21) is hard to miss. David too chose Solomon over older sons, but at God's word (1 Chronicles 28:5). Chronicles calls Rehoboam's handling of his sons "shrewd" in the next verse.

a: He was shrewd.
p: Rehoboam placed his other sons in the fortress towns, well supplied, away from the capital.
b: The verb bin means to understand or act with insight. Scattering the princes gave them positions and income, and kept them from plotting in Jerusalem, as Absalom and Adonijah had done in David's court. Abraham did something similar when he sent his other sons east with gifts (Genesis 25:6). The last phrase, "he asked for many wives," is unclear in Hebrew: most take it as wives for his sons (a mark of their rank), some as wives for himself.

a: Once Rehoboam's kingdom was firmly set
t: Set firm, but not his heart
p: The verb kun, 'make firm, make ready,' opens and closes Rehoboam's story: his kingdom was set, his heart was not.
b: 12:1 says Rehoboam's kingdom hekhin, "was established, made firm." 12:14 says he "had not made his heart ready" (lo hekhin libbo) to seek the LORD. The play on one verb sums up his reign. Chronicles then adds that "all Israel" left the law with him: here, as in 11:3, Israel means the people of Judah.

a: because they had acted unfaithfully toward the LORD
p: Kings reports Shishak's raid. Chronicles adds a reason: they had been unfaithful to the LORD.
b: Ma'al, "to act unfaithfully," is the word for breaking faith with God, used of Saul's death (1 Chronicles 10:13) and of the sins that led to the exile (1 Chronicles 9:1; 36:14). Chronicles turns the bare fact of Kings (1 Kings 14:25) into an example of its theology: sin brings judgment within the same generation, and here within a year or two of the people's turning away (11:17; 12:1). Most critical scholars call this the Chronicler's teaching of immediate retribution; see the topic.

a: Libyans, Sukkites and Cushites
p: Shishak was himself of Libyan descent. His army drew on Libya, Nubia and desert peoples.
b: Shoshenq I founded Egypt's 22nd Dynasty, a line of Libyan origin from the Delta. Libyans (Lubim) and Cushites (Nubians, from the Nile south of Egypt) served in Egyptian armies (Nahum 3:9). The Sukkites (Sukkiyyim) are known only here; the Greek (Rahlfs' edition, checked) calls them "Troglodytes," cave dwellers, perhaps of the Red Sea coast. The numbers of chariots and horsemen are much larger than other Egyptian armies of the time. On Shishak's own record of the campaign at Karnak, see the note on 1 Kings 14:25.

a: He captured the fortified towns that belonged to Judah
p: The towns Rehoboam had just fortified (11:5–12) fall to Shishak. Strength without faithfulness does not save.
b: Chronicles places the building of the forts in Rehoboam's first three good years (11:17) and their fall after his turning away. Shishak's list at Karnak names about 150 places, mostly in the north and the Negev, and Jerusalem itself is not clearly named; few of Rehoboam's towns can be found on it. Some scholars conclude that Rehoboam paid Shishak off before he reached Jerusalem, which fits 12:9. Others think parts of the list are lost. The theological point is clear either way: walls did not protect a people who had left the LORD.

a: You have left me, so I in turn have left you
p: The prophet's word mirrors the sin: they left God, so God left them.
b: The verb 'azav, "leave, abandon," appears in 12:1 for the people and here for God. Chronicles often states its teaching this way, through prophets: David had told Solomon, "Seek him, and he will let you find him. Leave him, and he will cast you aside forever" (1 Chronicles 28:9), and the prophets Azariah and Zechariah will say the same (15:2; 24:20). The pattern goes back to Deuteronomy 31:16–17. Kings has no prophet at Shishak's invasion; Shemaiah is the same man of God who stopped Rehoboam from war (11:2).

a: The LORD is in the right
p: The leaders admit that God is just in punishing them. Later prayers of confession use the same words.
b: Tsaddiq YHWH, "the LORD is righteous," is a confession that the judgment is deserved. Pharaoh said it in the plagues (Exodus 9:27). After the exile it became a fixed part of prayers of confession: "LORD, God of Israel, you are righteous" (Ezra 9:15, fresh rendering; compare Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:14; Lamentations 1:18). The king and the leaders humble themselves here, the first case in the book of the response God asked for in 7:14.

a: I will give them a little escape
p: The phrase can mean 'some deliverance' or 'deliverance soon.' Ezra used similar words for the return from exile.
b: Kim'at lifletah is "like a little for escape." It can mean partial rescue (they are spared, but not freed from Shishak) or rescue in a little while. The Greek (checked) has "as a little for salvation." Ezra's prayer uses the same pair of words, kim'at and peletah, for the small community back in Judah: "for just a short while," God "has let a band of survivors remain" and has "given us a little life again in our slavery" (Ezra 9:8). Chronicles' readers could see their own situation in Rehoboam's: spared, but still serving a foreign king.

a: Then they will know what it is to serve me
p: Judah will learn by experience the difference between serving God and serving foreign kings.
b: Deuteronomy warns that if Israel did not serve the LORD with joy, "you will serve the enemies the LORD sends against you" (Deuteronomy 28:48). Here the lesson is meant to teach: God's service is lighter than the kingdoms of the world. The irony is sharp after chapter 10, where the people rebelled because Solomon's "service" was too hard (10:4). For readers under Persian rule, who prayed "Here we are today: slaves! The land you gave our ancestors... here we are on it, slaves" (Nehemiah 9:36), the verse put their own servitude in the same light. Christians compare Jesus' saying that his yoke is easy to bear (Matthew 11:30).

a: Judah, too, still had good things in it
p: Even in a bad reign, Chronicles notes what was good. The phrase returns in Jehoshaphat's story.
b: The Hebrew is "and also in Judah there were good things." It may mean that some people in Judah still did good, which moved God to spare it, or that things went well in Judah again after the invasion. A prophet will use the same phrase of Jehoshaphat (19:3). Chronicles' judgments are rarely all black or all white.

a: He had not made his heart ready to seek the LORD.
p: Kings blames Judah. Chronicles blames Rehoboam, and names the root: he did not set his heart on God.
b: 1 Kings 14:22–24 says "Judah did what was evil," listing high places, standing stones, Asherah poles and shrine men. Chronicles drops the list and gives a mixed portrait: three good years (11:17), a turning away (12:1), humility under judgment (12:6), and a final verdict of evil because his heart was never fixed on seeking the LORD. Commentators note that this is the inner side of the outward sins Kings lists: worship follows the heart.

a: in the family records
p: The Hebrew lehityachesh, 'for enrolling by genealogy,' is obscure here. It may describe Iddo's work.
b: The verb hityachesh means to be registered in a genealogy, a word common in Chronicles, Ezra and Nehemiah (1 Chronicles 5:17; Ezra 2:62). Here it may describe the kind of record Iddo kept, or it may be misplaced. Translations vary: "dealing with genealogies," "in the genealogical records," or omit it. It shows at least that Chronicles thought of the prophets' writings as including lists of families, like its own first nine chapters.
